summary: This standards-track document defines the Security Event Token, a data structure for statements of fact from an issuer about a subject. These represent security events, such as the issuance or revocation of a credential. A SET is based on the JSON Web Token.

plainLanguage.summary: A Security Event Token is a small signed document that says something happened: a password was reset, a session ended, an account was disabled. One system sends it to another, and the second system checks it and decides what to do. The RFC fixes how the document is written down, so that any pair of systems can exchange one, and it is careful to say that the token reports a fact rather than giving an order.

questions: what is a security event token
how are security events shared between systems
what is the events claim in a set
how is a set different from an id token
how does the events claim work
subtitle: A signed statement that something security-relevant happened, for another system to act on.

tldr.problem: When one system does something security-relevant, such as resetting a password or revoking a token, other systems often need to know about it, for example so they can end their own sessions. Every pair of systems tends to invent its own private way of telling the other, and those private mechanisms rarely agree.
tldr.mechanism: The Security Event Token is a JSON Web Token with a reserved claim called events, whose value is a JSON object whose member names are URIs naming the events and whose member values are JSON objects holding the event data. The RFC profiles the JWT claims, defines the media type application/secevent+jwt, and states what a separate profiling specification must define for each kind of event.
tldr.outcome: A recipient can validate a token, read what happened, and decide for itself what to do about it. The RFC is explicit that a token is a statement of fact and not a command, and it gives concrete rules for making sure a token is not mistaken for an ID token or an access token.

facts.label: Explicit typing value
facts.value: secevent+jwt in the typ header parameter

facts.label: Events claim value
facts.value: a JSON object containing at least one member

today: RFC 8417 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2018, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the JSON Web Token in RFC 7519 and leaves the definition of each kind of event to separate profiling specifications.

sections.title: What a Security Event Token Is
sections.content:
This specification defines an extensible Security Event Token data structure that can be exchanged using protocols such as HTTP. It builds on the JSON Web Token format in order to provide a self-contained token that can be optionally signed using JSON Web Signature and optionally encrypted using JSON Web Encryption. It profiles the use of JWT for the purpose of issuing SETs and defines a base format that profiling specifications use to define actual events and their meanings, with non-normative example events showing how events can be constructed. The specification is scoped to security- and identity-related events, and although SETs may be used for other purposes, it only considers the security and privacy concerns relevant to identity and personal information.

The most important idea in the document is that security events are not commands issued between parties. A SET describes statements of fact from the perspective of an issuer about a subject, such as a web resource, a token, an IP address, or the issuer itself. These statements of fact represent a logical event that occurred directly to or about a security subject, for example a statement about the issuance or revocation of a token on behalf of a subject. A security subject may be permanent, such as a user account, or temporary, such as an HTTP session. A state change could describe a direct change of entity state, an implicit change, or a higher-level security statement such as the creation, modification or removal of a resource, the resetting or suspension of an account, the revocation of a security token before it expires, the logout of a user session, or an indication that a user has been given control of an email identifier previously controlled by another user.

While the state change is often triggered by a user agent or a security subsystem, the issuance and transmission of the event may happen asynchronously and in a back channel to the action that caused it. A recipient that receives a SET validates and interprets it and takes its own independent actions, if any: having been told that an email address is now used by someone else, it might choose not to grant the new user access to resources associated with the previous user, or it may have no relationship with the subject at all and take no action. The intent of the specification is therefore to define a syntax for statements of fact that recipients may interpret for their own purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: The token says what happened, not what to do. A system that receives one checks it and decides for itself whether to act, because the receiving system may have nothing to do with the subject at all, and different recipients will want to react differently.

sections.title: The Structure of a Token
sections.content:
A SET is a JWT data structure representing one or more related aspects of a security event that occurred to a subject. The JWT Claims Set has two levels. The top-level claims form the SET envelope; some are present in every SET and others are specific to particular profiles. Claims in the envelope SHOULD be registered in the JSON Web Token Claims registry, or be public or private claims as defined in the JWT specification.

The envelope claims that this specification profiles are used to validate the SET and to give information about the event data it carries. The events claim contains the event identifiers and the event-specific data expressed about the security subject, and its value MUST be a JSON object containing at least one member. The envelope MAY include event-specific or profile-specific data.

Each member of the events object is a name and value pair. The name is a URI string value, the event identifier, and the value is a JSON object known as the event payload, which contains claims that pertain to that event identifier and need not be registered as JWT claims. An event with no payload claims SHALL be represented as the empty JSON object.

When a SET contains several event identifiers, they represent multiple aspects of the same state transition that occurred to the security subject, and they are not intended to be used to aggregate distinct events about the same subject. Beyond that, the interpretation of such a token is out of scope for this specification, although profiling specifications may define their own rules. Possible uses include providing classification information such as threat type or level, adding to existing event representations, linking a potential series of events, and specific-purpose event URIs used between particular issuers and recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: The token has an outer part, the claims that identify the issuer and the audience, and one special claim called events. The events claim is an object whose member names are web addresses naming what happened, and whose values are objects holding the details. A member value may be empty when the name alone says everything.

sections.title: The Claims
sections.content:
Several claims from the JWT specification are profiled for use in SETs. The iss claim contains a string identifying the service provider publishing the token, and is REQUIRED. In some cases the issuer of the SET is not the issuer associated with the security subject, so implementers cannot assume the two are the same unless the profiling specification says so. The iat claim gives the time the SET was issued and is REQUIRED. The jti claim gives a unique identifier for the SET, which MUST be unique within a particular event feed and MAY be used by clients to track whether a SET has already been received; it is REQUIRED.

The aud claim carries one or more audience identifiers and is RECOMMENDED. The sub claim carries the principal that is the subject of the SET, usually the entity whose state was changed, for example an IP address that was added to a blacklist, a URI representing a modified user resource, or a token identifier for a revoked token; if it is used, the profiling specification MUST define the content and format semantics of the value. It is OPTIONAL, because for any given profile the principal may already be identified without a subject claim, and some profiles may convey subject information in the event payload instead.

The exp claim is the time after which the token must not be accepted for processing, and in the context of a SET that notion does not typically apply, because a SET represents something that has already occurred and is historical; its use is therefore NOT RECOMMENDED.

This specification defines three new claims. The events claim contains the set of event statements, and multiple event identifiers with the same value MUST NOT be used, nor may the claim be used to express multiple independent logical events. The txn claim is an optional string holding a unique transaction identifier, used to correlate several related JWTs. The toe claim gives the date and time at which the event occurred, as a NumericDate; omitting it means the issuer is not sharing an event time with the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: Three claims are always required: who issued the token, when, and a unique id for it. The audience is recommended, and the subject is optional because a profile may identify the subject another way. The expiry claim is discouraged, because a token that reports something already past does not need to stop working.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four non-normative examples. The first is a password reset event for a hypothetical System for Cross-domain Identity Management, which a receiver might use as a trigger to reset the active user agent sessions of the identified user. Its events claim names the SCIM URN for a password reset and a second URI that carries extra information such as the current count of resets, and the envelope carries the issuer, the subject as the SCIM resource URI that was affected, and the intended audiences.

The second is a logout token. Its events claim holds an empty object under the OpenID back-channel logout URI, and the sub and sid claims identify the subject that was logged out. At the time of writing this example corresponds to the logout token in the OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout specification.

The third is a consent event, where a fictional medical service collects consent and notifies other parties. The individual was originally authenticated through OpenID Connect, but the issuer of the security event is the application rather than the OpenID provider. The payload contains its own iss and sub values, which refer to the issuer of the security subject rather than to the SET issuer, and which are distinct from the top-level iss, which always refers to the issuer of the event.

The fourth is an account disabled event, corresponding at the time of writing to the OpenID RISC account disabled event. The parameters of the event are included in the event payload, in this case the reason, and the subject of the event is identified using a subject payload value which is itself a JSON object.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the same shape used for four different jobs: a password reset, a logout, a consent record and a disabled account. Note that the payload can carry its own issuer and subject, which refer to the subject of the event rather than to the party sending the token.

sections.title: What a Profiling Specification Must Define
sections.content:
Profiling specifications define actual SETs for particular use cases, and define the syntax and semantics of SETs conforming to their profile and the rules for validating them. They SHOULD define syntax, semantics, subject identification and validation.

Syntax covers the claims and values in the JWT Claims Set, which may come from the JWT specification, from this specification or from the profiling specification, and the contents and format of the event payload. Semantics define what the contents mean. Possibly most important is defining the procedures used to validate the SET issuer and to obtain the keys controlled by the issuer that were used for the cryptographic operations in the JWT; some profiles may define an algorithm for retrieving the issuer's keys that uses the iss claim value as its input. If a profile allows the JWT to be unsecured, the means by which the integrity of the JWT is ensured MUST be specified.

Subject identification must be defined, along with how to tell the event subject's issuer apart from the SET issuer where that applies. It is NOT RECOMMENDED for a profiling specification to use the sub claim where the subject is not globally unique and has a different issuer from the SET itself. Validation must clearly specify the steps a recipient performs to check that the token is syntactically and semantically valid.

A profile may also decide whether the events claim may hold several members and what processing to use in the single and multiple cases. Some profiles allow several event identifiers and tell recipients to ignore any they do not understand, which allows for extension; others allow several but require all to be understood for the token to be accepted; others require exactly one. All of these choices are within the scope of a profiling specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is the empty form. Each kind of event gets its own profile that fills it in: what the token must contain, what it means, how the recipient identifies the subject, and exactly which checks the recipient performs before believing it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because the JWT specification says that all claims that are not understood must be ignored, there is a risk that a SET is confused with another kind of JWT from the same issuer. Unless that confusion is prevented, an attacker who possesses a SET might use it where another kind of JWT is expected, or the other way round. A SET profile that could otherwise be interpreted as a valid ID Token, because it includes the required claims and valid issuer and audience values for an ID Token, MUST require that the exp claim not be present, so that valid ID Token implementations reject it. The RFC notes that explicit typing does not achieve this, because ID Token validation does not use the typ header value.

For access tokens, the RFC recommends prohibiting the exp claim, using a separate aud value to distinguish the SET recipient from the protected resource that is the audience of an access token, modifying access token validation to check for the presence of the events claim, and using explicit typing with validation that checks the typ header. For other kinds of JWT, the simplest way to prevent substitution is to require that the SET not include the claims that the target kind requires, for example omitting sip_callid or orig.

SETs may contain sensitive information, so methods for distributing events SHOULD require a transport-layer security mechanism. Parties MUST support TLS 1.2 or a higher version and MAY support additional transport mechanisms meeting its requirements, and the client MUST perform a TLS server certificate check. Security events distributed through third parties, or that carry personally identifiable information, MUST be encrypted using JWE or secured for confidentiality by other means. Unless the integrity of the JWT is ensured by other means, it MUST be signed using JWS by an issuer trusted to do so for the use case.

The specification defines no delivery mechanism, and implementers must consider what a delivery mechanism that is not secure or not assured implies: a SET may be end-to-end secured with JWE but, without mutual TLS, there is no assurance that the correct endpoint received it and could process it. It also defines no means of ordering multiple SETs, although order sometimes matters, for example in provisioning where an object cannot be modified before it is created, and not at all for a token revocation. Timestamps such as iat should be used with caution to define order, because distributed systems have clock skew, so time alone does not guarantee order. Timing also matters: a revocation token that arrives at the same moment as the user logs back in could cause the new session to be wrongly treated as logged out, so it may be more appropriate to revoke a specific session or token than to make a general statement about a user.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk to watch is a token being used where it should not be. The RFC's main tool is leaving out the expiry claim, because an ID token needs one and a security event token does not, so an ID token validator rejects the substituted token. It also insists on TLS and on signing or encrypting the token itself.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
If a SET is retained for audit purposes, its signature can be used to verify its authenticity. SET issuers SHOULD attempt to specialise their tokens so that their content is targeted to the specific business and protocol needs of the intended recipients. When sharing personally identifiable information, or information that is otherwise confidential to affected users, issuers and recipients should have the appropriate legal agreements and user consent or terms of service in place.

The propagation of subject identifiers can be perceived as personally identifiable information, so where possible issuers and recipients SHOULD devise approaches that prevent it, for example passing a salted hash value that requires the recipient to know the subject. A recipient may also be able to correlate different events and thereby learn about a subject that the issuer did not intend to share: for instance, the recipient might use iat values or highly precise toe values to determine that two otherwise unrelated events are really the same real-world event, and the combination could let the recipient de-anonymise data or recognise that unrelated identifiers belong to the same individual. Issuers SHOULD take steps to minimise the chance of such correlation where it would be a privacy violation, for instance by using approximate values for the toe claim or by arbitrarily delaying the issuance of a token where such delay can be tolerated.
sections.plainLanguage: Two tokens that say nothing identifying can still be put together to find out who a person is, if their timings are exact enough. The RFC therefore says to keep the event time approximate where it can, to delay sending a token where that is tolerable, and to pass a salted hash rather than a raw identifier where the recipient already knows the subject.

items.title: Issuer
items.text: The service provider that creates the SET and sends it to a recipient.

items.title: Recipient
items.text: The entity that receives the SET through some distribution method and interprets it.

items.title: Subject
items.text: The thing the event happened to: a principal, a web resource, an IP address, or the issuer itself.

items.title: Event identifier
items.text: A URI naming the event. It is the member name inside the events object.

items.title: Event payload
items.text: A JSON object holding the claims for that event. It may be empty.

items.title: Profiling specification
items.text: A document that defines one kind of event, its claims and the rules for checking it.

viz.caption: THE CLAIMS AND HOW REQUIRED THEY ARE

cells: The service provider publishing the SET.
The time the SET was issued.
A unique identifier for the SET, used to track whether it has already been received.
The principal the event is about. The profile must define its format if it is used.
The date and time the event occurred, as a NumericDate.
A transaction identifier for correlating related JWTs.
The time after which the token must not be accepted. A SET is historical, so it rarely applies.

viz.caption: HOW TO KEEP A TOKEN FROM BEING MISUSED

items.title: Leave out exp
items.text: A SET that could pass as an ID token must not carry exp, since exp is required in an ID token and so the substituted token is rejected.

items.title: Use a separate audience
items.text: Where possible, give the SET recipient a different aud value from the protected resource that is the audience of an access token.

items.title: Check for the events claim
items.text: Make access token validation reject any JWT carrying an events claim, and require one for SETs.

items.title: Use explicit typing
items.text: Set the typ header to secevent+jwt, and have the validation system check it.

items.title: Omit what the other token needs
items.text: For other JWT types, leave out the claims that type requires, so a substituted SET is rejected.
